author: Al Jazeera English
description:
Mark Pfeifle, a former US national security advisor and president of Off the Record Strategies, joins Al Jazeera from Washington, DC, to assess Trump's threat of "total economic warfare" against Iran. He says the real test is China, which has cut its Iranian oil imports from roughly 1.5 million to 500,000 barrels a day since the war began, diversifying toward Brazil, Iraq and Russia, though it's unclear if that shift will last. Trump has sanctioned 60 entities but not yet banks.

Pfeifle warns that success requires tracking money as quickly as Iran and China move it through crypto, shell companies, and shadow banks, since sanctioning one channel just pushes funds elsewhere. Directly sanctioning Chinese institutions could further pressure Beijing, but Washington is reluctant, given intertwined trade ties and a Trump-Xi summit next month. He says China is playing a long game, content to see the US tied down in the Middle East while buying discounted Iranian oil.

title: Will Trump's Iran sanctions actually work this time? Analysis

author: Al Jazeera English
description:
Alok Bohara, professor emeritus of economics at the University of New Mexico and founding director of the Nepal Study Centre, joins Al Jazeera from Albuquerque. He describes a personal connection to the devastated region, having trekked as a student to Timure near the China border, a village he says has now been completely wiped out along with the community hub of Syabrubesi.

Bohara says roughly $4 to $5 billion in pledged aid, nearly a tenth of Nepal's GDP, is significant, but argues the country needs to "rethink," not just rebuild. He says Nepal adopted political federalism without ever developing an equivalent for ecological risk and planning. The floods exposed engineering risk from fragile mountain terrain, investment risk after six or seven hydropower plants, representing 10 to 12 percent of national capacity, and 40 kilometres of trade roads to China were destroyed, and household risk from building too close to rivers, which he says calls for solutions like flood insurance.

Catastrophic floods, snow and mudslides have struck the Andes region, with Chile, Peru and Bolivia all badly hit. Peru's president has declared a state of emergency as experts warn that up to 1.2 million people could be affected.

In northern Chile's Atacama Desert, sudden mudslides swept away vehicles and sent residents fleeing. Evacuee Sergio Vargas describes the Coloso ravine surging without warning after the rain had stopped. In Bolivia, unprecedented snowstorms in the Andes are threatening tens of thousands of llamas and sheep, with herder Elizabeth Calle moving starving animals to lower ground in search of food. In Peru, days of torrential rain have triggered landslides, destroying homes and leaving thousands displaced.

Reporting from central Chile, Al Jazeera's Lucia Newman notes melting Andes snow and another storm front forecast this weekend could bring fresh flooding, with the region's usual rainy season still to come.

But as Al Jazeera's Manny Rapalo reports from the White House, military superiority hasn't ended the war, leaving officials facing a harder question: what now counts as victory? Trump insists the military campaign was actually faster than the six weeks promised, and argues securing a political agreement with Tehran is separate from military success. Restoring safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz remains unresolved.

author: Al Jazeera English
description:
Alton Byers, a mountain geographer at the University of Colorado Boulder's Institute of Arctic and Alpine Research, joins Al Jazeera to explain the ongoing risk from Nepal's glacial lakes. He says newly formed lakes, held back only by loose debris from the recent glacier collapse, could spill over with little warning. Natural drainage is possible, or teams could attempt to drain them manually, as has been done in Peru, though Byers warns that this poses a real risk of triggering a sudden glacial lake outburst flood.

He says the initial collapse likely wasn't caused by an earthquake but by warming permafrost, a trend that has accelerated since the Industrial Revolution and is now destabilising even the highest mountain terrain, making massive ice and rock breaks more frequent.

US President Donald Trump says the US has struck the "biggest oil deal in world history" with Venezuela, claiming US companies have secured majority control of more than 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan oil reserves at no cost to taxpayers, a move he says could more than double US reserves and lower fuel prices. Energy economist Ed Hirs, of the University of Houston, joins Al Jazeera from New York to assess the claim.

Hirs says having reserves in the ground is not the same as extracting them. Venezuela has repeatedly nationalised foreign oil assets, and most major companies still see the country as uninvestable given weak rule of law, including recent imprisonment of oil executives. Production has collapsed from over 3 million barrels a day to roughly 1 million, and extraction costs run $70 to $75 a barrel. description:
What caused Nepal's deadly flash floods, what's now threatening rescue efforts, and how can it be stopped from happening again? Analysts say a huge chunk of glacier plunged more than a kilometre into a valley near the Nepal-China border, sending walls of water through communities below and leaving more than 1,000 people reported missing.

The collapse left behind debris that has formed unstable "barrier lakes," held back only by weak walls of loose rock. If those walls give way, millions of cubic litres of water could surge downstream, adding to the danger already posed by glacial lakes scattered across the Himalayas, some formed as melting glaciers leave deep holes that fill with water, others dammed by soil pushed up by moving ice. A 2022 study found climate change has increased glacial avalanches and landslides, causing more of these lakes to burst their banks.
